question: After a seed investor's lawyer sent our Delaware corporation a demand letter, my co-founder left auto-delete switched on in the team chat app, and about four months of messages are gone and cannot be pulled from any backup. The investor has since sued in federal court. Can the judge tell the jury to presume the deleted messages would have hurt us, and what would the court have to find first?

In a federal lawsuit over a disputed SAFE conversion, the investor has asked for every personal text message I sent to anyone over the last seven years, arguing that anything might turn out to be relevant. What is the standard for how far discovery can reach, and what factors can I point to when pushing back?

A seed investor suing our startup in federal court served document requests for the cap table spreadsheets and board decks but did not say what format they want. Can we just print everything to flat PDFs, and if we produce in one format, can they later make us produce the same files again in native form?

In our federal case, my co-founder subpoenaed the outside law firm that handled our seed round for its files on the founders' vesting schedule. The firm wants to hold back privileged emails. What does it have to provide about what it withholds, and what happens if it hands over a privileged email by mistake?

At our Rule 26(f) conference in a federal investor-founder case, the other side wants to put off any discussion of privilege logs until all documents are produced. Do the current federal rules require the discovery plan to address when and how privilege logs will be served?

In a federal case between me and a seed investor, our paralegal accidentally included an email from our corporate counsel giving legal advice about my vesting in a 4,000-page production. We had a privilege review in place and caught the mistake two days later. Have we waived privilege, and what must we have done to keep it?

Our counsel and the co-founder's counsel signed a letter agreeing that any privileged document produced by mistake will be returned with no waiver. If a different investor later sues us in state court and argues that a document we produced in this federal case lost its privilege, does the letter agreement protect us, or do we need something from the federal judge?

We are in the District of Colorado, and the co-founder's lawyer has ignored our requests to talk about his incomplete document production. Before we file a motion to compel, what does the local rule require us to do, and do we have to show the court what we did?

Our founder dispute in the District of Colorado has a scheduling conference on the calendar. Do we have to file a separate written Rule 26(f) discovery-plan report, and how far ahead of the scheduling conference is the proposed scheduling order due?
mustNot: scheduling order (is |must be |shall be )?(due|tendered|filed|submitted) (no later than )?(14|fourteen|21|twenty-one) days before

question: In the District of Delaware, we want to file a motion to compel against a co-founder who has out-of-state lead counsel and local Delaware counsel. Our lead lawyers have traded emails with theirs about the dispute. Is that enough to satisfy the meet-and-confer requirement for a nondispositive motion?

In a District of Delaware case with a seed investor, no Rule 502 non-waiver order has been entered yet, and we just realized we produced a privileged board memo three weeks ago. Under the court's default discovery standard, how long do we have to give notice and get it back?

We are litigating with a co-founder in the District of Delaware and have not agreed on an ESI protocol. He wants every file produced natively, and we would rather produce images. What production format applies by default, and which files go out in native form?

Our dispute with a co-founder is in the Delaware Court of Chancery. After it was clear litigation was coming but before suit was filed, he deleted a shared drive of product files that cannot be recovered. Does the Court of Chancery have to find he intended to deprive us of the files before it can presume they were unfavorable to him, or is a lower standard enough?

No lawsuit has been filed yet, but a co-founder has written that he will sue in the Delaware Court of Chancery over a disputed stock repurchase. Do we have to start preserving electronic records now, and what steps does the Court expect, for example for personal email accounts and home laptops?

A seed investor sued our Delaware corporation in the Court of Chancery and served document requests together with the summons and complaint. When are our written responses to the document requests due?

In our Court of Chancery case, the other founder's privilege log uses the same line, 'email reflecting legal advice,' for hundreds of entries, including emails where a lawyer was only copied. Is that acceptable in Chancery, and do we have to log our own communications with litigation counsel after the complaint was filed?
